results.content:
People rarely write code by hand anymore. AI often reviews it too, and software moves so fast that reading every line is hard. Still, I'm sure of one thing: understanding code matters as much as ever. And understanding code means learning how a senior engineer thinks. That is what lets you give AI the right instructions, notice what really matters in a problem, design well, and keep a project moving in the right direction.

So diff-tour teaches that thinking on real changes. Point it at a branch, and the AI coding CLI you already use writes a tour of the change. Then you step through it with → and ←:

   What the change is for, and which files to read next, including ones that didn't change [...] , what must be fixed and what is a nit, and where they'd say "wait", asked as questions so you guess first. Runs on your AI coding CLI. Read-only, open source.

Getting started is just this: install with the one-line script in the README, then run it in any git repository:

```
cd your-repo
tour
```

The first run asks for a language and an AI CLI, with recommended choices already selected. Press Enter three times and the tour starts being written.

Things I cared about:

   It's read-only. The AI gets a copy of the files git tracks and read-only tools, enforced by command-line flags, not only by the prompt

results.title: Teach Your AI to Think Like a Senior Engineer
results.content:
For example, when I needed to implement Cora’s email bankruptcy feature—clearing 53,000-email inboxes without deleting anything important—I didn’t start by coding. I created a research agent to plan instead.

I thought this would be an easy feature. Bulk archive 53,000 emails—how hard could it be? I asked the research agent to analyze our own bulk operation patterns, check API limits for mass actions, and propose three implementation approaches with tradeoffs. [...] The best-practices agent found: the library's official documentation, changelogs (lists of what changed between versions), and upgrade guides showing how to move my code to the new version—all with source links automatically included.
